extraction.name: HELVIPAD
extraction.description: A real-world dataset for omnidirectional stereo depth estimation featuring paired top-bottom 360° images with corresponding depth and disparity labels, captured in indoor and outdoor scenes under varied lighting conditions, with augmented training data via depth completion.
extraction.creator: Mehdi Zayene; Jannik Endres; Albias Havolli; Charles Corbiere; Salim Cherkaoui; Alexandre Kontouli; Alexandre Alahi
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data were collected on a university campus using a custom-built robot rig with two Ricoh Theta V 360° cameras in a top-bottom setup and a synchronized Ouster OS1-64 LiDAR sensor, capturing indoor and outdoor scenes under varied lighting and weather conditions.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Ground-truth depth labels are sparse because LiDAR point clouds cover only a fraction of image pixels.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consist of synchronized top and bottom 360° camera images and LiDAR point clouds.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: LiDAR point clouds were projected onto equirectangular images to obtain depth maps and disparity maps; images and labels were cropped to remove unnecessary borders, and one out of every three camera frames was retained to match the LiDAR frame rate.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Depth and disparity labels were automatically generated by projecting LiDAR point clouds onto equirectangular images, and an augmented training set was created using a fully automated depth completion pipeline.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper evaluates LiDAR-image alignment with pixel error and validates depth completion by splitting each LiDAR point cloud into training and test sets and computing depth estimation metrics on the test set.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to support development of depth estimation models for robotic navigation and interaction in dynamic human environments.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset is collected on a university campus, and indoor-trained models generalize poorly to outdoor scenes, especially at night; the depth completion method is also limited for fast-moving objects like cars.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset was collected on a university campus; LiDAR depth maps are sparse; depth completion is limited for fast-moving objects like cars; and indoor-trained models show limited generalization to outdoor scenes, particularly at night.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is used for training, validation, and testing stereo depth estimation models for omnidirectional images, and serves as a benchmark for assessing robustness across diverse lighting conditions and depth ranges.

name.evidence: We introduce HELVIPAD, a comprehensive real-world dataset for stereo depth estimation from 360° images.

inLanguage.evidence: HELVIPAD : A Real-World Dataset for Omnidirectional Stereo Depth Estimation

rai:dataCollection.evidence: To assemble a dataset capturing human pedestrian activity, we built a custom rig and collected data across distinct scenes, encompassing indoor ( e.g., corridors, halls) and outdoor ( e.g., squares, extemal parking, footpaths) settings in various lighting conditions on a university campus.

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: Data were collected using a custom-built rig equipped with two omnidirectional cameras in a vertical arrangement, which prevents occlusion, and paired with a synchronized LiDAR sensor to provide high-quality depth measurements.

rai:dataCollectionMissingData.evidence: Given the sparse nature of LiDAR point clouds compared to high-resolution camera images, ground-truth depth labels cover only a fraction of the total pixels.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: Each sequence is synchronized with its corresponding LiDAR point clouds, which are projected on frames to obtain depth maps, and subsequently disparity maps.

rai:dataCollectionTimeframe.evidence: The HELVIPAD dataset includes 26 video sequences captured between December 2023 and February 2024., recorded at a frame rate of 10 Hz.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: Each sequence is synchronized with its corresponding LiDAR point clouds, which are projected on frames to obtain depth maps, and subsequently disparity maps. Top images, bottom images, depth maps, and disparity maps are then cropped to remove unnecessary borders and downsized from a width of 1024 pixels to 512 to enable more efficient training.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: Collected using two 360° cameras in a top-bottom setup and a LiDAR sensor, the dataset includes accurate depth and disparity labels by projecting 3D point clouds onto equirectangular images.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: To assess alignment accuracy, we calculated the pixel error by measuring Euclidean distances between 200 randomly selected LiDAR points and their image positions [29], resulting in an average error of 1.7 pixels.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: KISS-ICP [33] is one of the state-of-the-art approaches for LiDAR odometry.

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: Mobile robots are increasingly used in real-world applications such as autonomous driving [18], healthcare [20], or agriculture [12], where accurate 3D representations of dynamic human environments are crucial for navigation and interaction.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: While collected on a university campus, the dataset captures many common urban environments, such as parking lots, roads, underpasses, pedestrian squares, footpaths, corridors and crowded halls.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: Given this limited temporal window, the error introduced by the movement of the robot, or within the scene, is negligible, given the LiDAR’s high frame rate and the rig’s sub-pedestrian moving speed (see Appendix C.3). Note that this approach is limited for fast-moving objects like cars.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: To create the benchmark, we split the captured sequences into a train-val set and a test set, ensuring the same proportion of outdoor ,indoor andnight outdoor sequences.
